Ecosystem tool request: The participant asks for a new or changed tool that connects ADI tools with each other or with third-party tools.
Power specific pain: A problem that only shows up in power design work: regulators, power budgets, thermal or efficiency trade-offs.
Power tool request: A request for a feature or tool for power design work.
Precision tool request: A request for a feature or tool for precision signal-chain work: ADCs, DACs, amplifiers, references.
RF specific pain: A problem that only shows up in RF design work: matching, link budgets, frequency planning, RF parts.
RF tool request: A request for a feature or tool for RF design work.
AI attempted: The participant tried an AI assistant or AI feature for engineering work, whatever the outcome.
AI future potential: Where the participant thinks AI could help them in future; hopes and imagined uses, not current use.
AI skepticism: Doubts about AI for engineering: accuracy, trust, liability, or not wanting it at all.
Data sheet friction: Trouble finding, reading or trusting information in a data sheet.
Data sheet positive: Praise for a data sheet: clear, complete, or better than other vendors'.
Feedback mechanism missing: The participant found an error or gap but had no easy way to report it to ADI.
Specification depth valued: The participant values detailed specs, typical-performance curves or test conditions.
Search gave up: The participant stopped searching on the website or in a tool without finding what they wanted.
Site findability friction: Difficulty navigating the website or finding a product, tool or document on it.
Site findability positive: Something on the website was easy to find, or navigation worked well.
Cross-vendor comparison: Comparing ADI parts or tools with another vendor's, or switching between vendors' tools.
Demo board used: The participant used an evaluation or demo board to try or validate a part.
Internal library first: The participant starts part selection from their company's approved or internal parts library.
Selection friction: Difficulty choosing a part: too many options, unclear filters, missing parameters.
Delight: Clear enthusiasm or pleasant surprise about a product, tool or experience.
Frustration: Clear annoyance or exasperation, whatever its cause.
Skepticism: General doubt that a claim, product or tool will work as promised (for AI doubts use AI skepticism).
Trust: The participant says they trust, or rely on, ADI, a tool or a data source, and why.
FAE as differentiator: Field application engineers or direct support are named as a reason to choose ADI.
Support friction: Slow, unhelpful or hard-to-reach technical support.
Support positive: Support that was fast, knowledgeable or went beyond expectations.
Block Diagramming specific pain: A problem specific to block-diagramming tools or drawing system block diagrams.
Block Diagramming tool request: A request for a feature in a block-diagramming tool.
Ecosystem specific pain: A problem caused by tools not working together: formats, exports, missing integrations.
Excel as primary tool: The participant does design calculations or tracking in spreadsheets instead of a dedicated tool.
External tool preferred: The participant prefers a non-ADI tool for a task, and says why.
Precision specific pain: A problem that only shows up in precision signal-chain work: noise, drift, error budgets.
Simulation gap: A simulation or model the participant needed was missing, wrong or not detailed enough.
Tool friction: A usability problem or bug in an ADI design tool.
Tool positive: Praise for an ADI design tool.
Multi-tool handoff: Work has to move between several tools by hand: copying values, re-entering data, exporting files.
Rework required: Work had to be redone because of an error, a missing feature or a late change.
Stage naming mismatch: The participant names a design stage differently from how ADI or its tools name it.
Workflow ad hoc: The participant has no fixed process for a task and improvises each time.
Workflow described: The participant walks through how they do a task, step by step.
